title: Why TSMC Is Building Memory Above Processor Logic
author: F
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

TSMC’s research into back-end-of-line (BEOL) memory points to a promising way to bring more data closer to processors. Instead of manufacturing memory solely as separate chips, the approach embeds memory cells within the interconnect layers above a processor’s logic circuitry. TSMC demonstrated this integration at the 2025 Symposium on VLSI Technology and Circuits, positioning it as a denser alternative to SRAM for cache applications.

The design uses one transistor and one capacitor per memory cell, with an oxide-semiconductor transistor and a capacitor manufactured through a low-temperature process. TSMC’s research paper reports operation at 0.75 volts, random memory cycles below eight nanoseconds, and data retention exceeding 128 milliseconds at 85°C. These are encouraging research results, although they do not establish readiness for commercial production.

Why does the processor’s footprint matter? Integrating memory above logic potentially lets designers spread storage across the processor’s available area. For a given capacity, that could reduce the number of memory layers required compared with building over a smaller footprint. However, usable area, wiring, heat, and manufacturing constraints will determine the actual advantage.

The broader significance is the possibility of easing the memory bottleneck. AI processors need rapid access to enormous amounts of data. More nearby memory could reduce transfers to external memory, potentially improving performance and energy efficiency. Denser caches could also give chip designers greater flexibility when balancing computing resources against storage capacity.

However, embedded BEOL memory should not be confused with a confirmed move into standalone commodity DRAM manufacturing. The report interprets TSMC’s statement reaffirming its foundry focus as leaving room for memory development, but that wording does not confirm a commercial roadmap.

What matters now is whether TSMC can translate the demonstrated technology into reliable, economical manufacturing at scale, while meeting customers’ requirements for speed, capacity, power consumption, and integration.
